15 Key Accounting and Tax Stories for CFOs

Introduction

This morning's press review from Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications brings you 15 essential stories on accounting, tax, and corporate secretarial affairs that every professional needs to know. Our media monitoring across 13 major dailies reveals critical developments in GST, corporate governance, and fiscal policy that demand your attention.

1. Uniform GST Registration Guidelines on the Horizon
A front-page report in Economic Times says the Centre and state tax officers are working on guidelines to bring uniformity in documents submitted for faster processing of GST registration, requiring businesses to pass on tax credit exceeding two point five lakhs monthly. Once agreed upon, the proposal will be placed before the GST Council, chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.
Why it matters: Streamlined GST registration reduces compliance friction for high-credit businesses.
Key detail: Centre and states are standardising document requirements for registrations where monthly ITC exceeds Rs 2.5 lakh. Proposal goes to GST Council next.
Source: Economic Times
Next step: CFOs of eligible firms should prepare digital documentation to benefit from faster approvals.

2. GSTAT Sees Only One-Third of Expected Cases
A front-page report in Indian Express says only about one-third of the expected 2.5 lakh cases have been filed at the Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) since September last year. The lukewarm response from taxpayers has concerned GST Appellate Tribunal President Justice(Retd) Sanjaya Kumar Mishra, who expressed disappointment over the lower number of case filings.
Why it matters: Low filing volume suggests taxpayers may be avoiding the appellate route or settling disputes earlier.
Key detail: Only 74,758 cases filed against an expected 2.5 lakh. Justice Mishra expresses disappointment.
Source: Indian Express, Economic Times
Next step: Review pending GST disputes – GSTAT may offer faster resolution if case load remains low.

3. ₹7,185 Crore Pan Masala Tax Evasion Uncovered
A front-page report in The Pioneer says DGGI officers busted a clandestine pan masala and tobacco manufacturing network in Uttar Pradesh, seizing 27 undeclared pouch-packing machines and detecting tax evasion of about 7185 crore. The operation uncovered 15.5 lakh pouches of finished goods and substantial raw materials, with the proprietor arrested under the HSNS Act and Central Excise Act.
Why it matters: DGGI's crackdown signals heightened enforcement on unregistered manufacturing.
Key detail: 27 pouch-packing machines seized, 15.5 lakh pouches recovered, proprietor arrested.
Source: The Pioneer
Next step: Assess supply chain compliance for tobacco and pan masala products.

4. Audit Flags ₹1.69 Crore NPA Paid to Admin Doctors
A sample audit of the Health Department has found that Rs 1.69 crore in non-practicing allowance (NPA) was paid to 16 doctors while they were serving in administrative positions. The 16 doctors include five Civil Surgeons, seven Deputy Civil Surgeons and four medical officers. The NPA was paid from June 2018 to December 2025. As per the audit objection, Rs 1,68,98,342 was paid to various Deputy Civil Surgeons/Surgeons while they were serving in administrative positions from 2018-19 (June 2018) to 2025-26 (December 2025). The audit added that records related to the clinical duties performed by the Deputy Civil Surgeons/Surgeons concerned were not submitted to it, making it impossible to ascertain whether they actually performed clinical duties. It said NPA was granted only if these doctors performed clinical duties alongside their adminis-trative work. Vide a letter dated July 21, a reply was sought from the doctors as to whether they had performed any clinical duty from June 2018 to December 2025. However, the Haryana Civil Medical Services Association (HCMSA) came out in support of the 16 doctors on Friday. The Haryana Civil Services (Allowances) Rules, 2016, define NPA as an allowance granted to specified categories of government doctors in lieu of private practice. Subsequently, the Finance Department, vide an order dated June 20, 2018, prescribed the conditions governing its admissibility. "Neither the statutory Rules nor the Finance Department notification altered the fundamental object of NPA, which is compensation for the prohibition imposed upon government doctors from engaging in private medical practice," said the association’s letter to the Principal Accountant General, Haryana. The association said the present interpretation adopted in the audit observation appeared to rest solely on the criterion that only doctors directly engaged in clinical duties were entitled to NPA, which was not justified as it ignored the very purpose of the grant of NPA. "A government doctor does not lose scope of doing private practice merely because the government assigns him or her responsibilities relating to disease control programmes, public health administration, technical supervision, monitoring, training, surveillance, field visits or implementation of National Health Programmes," said HCMSA president Dr Anil Yadav. He added, "The restriction against private practice remains equally applicable irrespective of the nature of government duty assigned, because every such doctor has ample scope to do private practice; hence they too are entitled to NPA." The association pointed out that "NPA is granted to all doctors in medical colleges, AYUSH and Veterinary doctors not only in Haryana, but in central government institutes and other states irrespective of their nature of duties."
Why it matters: Non-practicing allowance granted without clinical duty proof raises governance questions.
Key detail: 16 doctors received NPA from 2018–2025 while in administrative roles. HCMSA contests audit interpretation.
Source: Tribune
Next step: Public sector CFOs should review allowance compliance in health departments.

5. Easing Blocked GST Credit on Self-Used Construction
A front-page report in Business Standard says that the government is examining industry concerns over the denial of input tax credit (ITC) on goods and services used to construct immovable property for its own use, according to a senior government official. The issue is being discussed with states, but no agreement has been reached yet on easing the restriction.
Why it matters: Potential unlock of significant ITC for real estate and manufacturing firms.
Key detail: Government discussing removal of restriction on goods/services used to build own property. States yet to agree.
Source: Business Standard
Next step: Monitor GST Council updates – early movers can plan capital expenditure accordingly.

6. Over 65 Million Tax Returns Filed for AY 2026-27
A front-page report in Financial Express says that over 65 million income tax ‘returns’ have already been filed for Assessment Year 2O26-27, the tax department said on Friday. These include over 2O million ITR-3 and ITR-4 returns as of August 2O. Last date to file ITR-3, 4,5 and 7 (non-audit) is August 3l.
Why it matters: Robust filing numbers indicate improving taxpayer compliance.
Key detail: 20 million ITR-3 and ITR-4 filed by Aug 20. Deadline for non-audit returns: Aug 31.
Source: Financial Express
Next step: Ensure timely filing to avoid late fees – especially for ITR-3/4 filers.

7. Oil India Announces 67th AGM
Oil India Limited has announced its 67th Annual General Meeting (AGM) to be held virtually on September 17, 2026. Members are invited to participate via Video Conferencing (VC) or Other Audio-Visual Means (OAVM). The company has also extended a record date for dividend eligibility of September 4, 2026, and is requesting shareholders to submit necessary documents for KYC compliance.
Why it matters: Corporate secretarial teams must prepare for virtual AGM compliance.
Key detail: Meeting on Sept 17 via VC, record date Sept 4 for dividend.
Source: Business Standard
Next step: Shareholders should complete KYC documents for participation.

8. Sugar Mills Push for Early Crushing, Seek GST Relief
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says cooperative sugar mills are targeting an early start to crushing operations by October 15, subject to state approvals, to bolster supplies ahead of peak festival demand. The National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories warned that premature crushing could shave sugar recovery by 2 to 3 percent, squeezing mill economics, and has sought GST relief on October–November sales and soft loans.
Why it matters: Early start can meet festive demand but risks lower recovery.
Key detail: NFCSF warns 2–3% recovery loss; seeks GST concession on Oct–Nov sales and soft loans.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Sugar industry CFOs should evaluate margin impact of early crushing vs. market timing.

9. ₹9 Crore Cash Seized en Route to Tamil Nadu
A front-page report in Deccan Herald says Rs 9 crore in cash was intercepted by Bengaluru police on the southern outskirts of the city. According to the police report, on August 18, they received information from Jagadish, Deputy Director of Income Tax, Unit-22, Bengaluru, that a large amount of cash was being illegally transported in a Hyundai Creta (KL 2OT 8629). The car was headed to Hosur in Tamil Nadu from Bengaluru.
Why it matters: Highlights income tax scrutiny on unaccounted cash movement.
Key detail: IT department tip led to interception of Hyundai Creta carrying illegal cash.
Source: Deccan Herald
Next step: Review cash handling policies and ensure all large movements are documented.

10. CAG Warns of Rising Fiscal Risks in Rajasthan
A front-page report in First India says the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) 2024-25 State Finances Audit Report flagged concerns over Rajasthan’s fiscal health, citing a rising fiscal deficit, higher debt-servicing burden, increased reliance on market borrowings despite strong economic growth.
Why it matters: State debt burden and fiscal deficit metrics affect project financing and credit ratings.
Key detail: CAG 2024-25 report flags higher debt servicing and market borrowing reliance despite GSDP growth.
Source: First India
Next step: Firms with Rajasthan exposure should monitor state's fiscal health indicators.

11. Mining Tax Amendments Raise Federal Concerns
A front-page report in Statesman says that the proposed amendments to the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 seek to bring greater transparency, uniformity, and predictability to mineral taxation. However, the attempt to restrict State taxation of mineral-bearing land raises a legitimate constitutional and federal concern.
Why it matters: Changes to mineral taxation may alter state vs centre revenue balance.
Key detail: Proposed amendments to MMDR Act aim for uniformity but may restrict state powers.
Source: Statesman
Next step: Mining companies should assess impact on royalty and cess structures.

12. Karnataka CM Urges CAs to Boost Revenue Mobilisation
A front-page report in Deccan Herald says... Chief Minister DK Shivakumar inaugurated SAMVAADA 2O26, a two-day conference in Bengaluru on Friday. He urged chartered accountants to advise the state government on improving revenue mobilisation, plugging leakages and correcting financial lapses without burdening businesses.
Why it matters: State seeking professional input to plug leakages without burdening businesses.
Key detail: DK Shivakumar inaugurates SAMVAADA 2026, calls for innovative tax suggestions from CAs.
Source: Deccan Herald
Next step: CA firms in Karnataka can contribute to policy proposals and gain visibility.

13. Tax Guide: Build House Within 3 Years to Save LTCG
A front-page report in Financial Express says taxpayers can save long-term capital gains tax under Section 82 of the Income-tax Act by constructing a house within three years of asset transfer. Writers discuss home loan interest deductions, gift transfers, and reinvestment rules.
Why it matters: Section 82 of Income-tax Act offers capital gains exemption on reinvestment.
Key detail: Home loan interest deductions, gift transfers, and reinvestment rules explained.
Source: Financial Express
Next step: Taxpayers planning real estate sale should time reinvestment for maximum benefit.

14. IndAS 17 Set to Transform Insurance Reporting
A front-page report in Business Standard says IndAS 17 is set to transform financial reporting for Indian insurers. The new accounting standard, aligned with IFRS 17, will replace dual reporting frameworks and bring uniformity, transparency, and better disclosure of economic profits.
Why it matters: New standard aligns Indian insurers with IFRS 17, enhancing transparency.
Key detail: Replaces dual reporting framework, brings uniformity and better economic profit disclosure.
Source: Business Standard
Next step: Insurance CFOs should ensure systems are ready for the transition timeline.

15. HP State Corporation Invites CA Firm Tenders
A front-page report in Tribune says the Himachal Pradesh State Industrial Development Corporation Limited is inviting online bids through electronic tendering system for the appointment of Chartered Accountancy firms. The tenders are required for the period Oct-26 to Mar-28.
Why it matters: Opportunity for CA firms to secure government audit and compliance contracts.
Key detail: Tenders for Oct 2026 – Mar 2028 period via e-tendering.
Source: Tribune
Next step: Eligible firms should submit bids before deadline.

Closing

This media intelligence from Press Monitor keeps you ahead of regulatory shifts and business risks. Which story will impact your organisation first? Share your thoughts in the comments – we read every one.

🔥 MUST-REMEMBER FACTS

India has ~150 million people above 60; projected to reach 347 million by 2050.

TFR: 1.9, below replacement level.

Digital fraud increasingly threatens elderly citizens.

I think the BJP is misdiagnosing the challenge it faces with younger Indians.

The assumption seems to be that this is primarily a communication problem: more Instagram reels, more vertical video, younger lingo, a different style of addressing people.

But that is a first-order response to a much deeper shift on the ground.

Gen Z does not necessarily want political leaders to imitate its language or aesthetic. In fact, trying too hard to do so can make leadership look less authentic.

The problem is not style. It is content.

PM Modi’s great political strength over the last 25 years has been his ability to combine remarkable continuity with constant reinvention: the core remains identifiable, but every few years there is a sense of a new mission.

That was also supported by decades of ideological clarity within the broader ecosystem on issues such as Article 370, Ram Mandir and the UCC.

Many of those longstanding objectives are now either accomplished or substantially advanced.

So the natural question is: what is the next big agenda?

For younger India, I would put three issues near the top. They relate emotionally and intellectually to these 3 issues. Addressing them will naturally connect the BJP with them. 

1. Urban governance

For far too long, Indians have accepted cities that are congested, polluted, poorly planned and increasingly difficult to live in.

The Smart Cities Mission had the right ambition, even if its outcomes were uneven. That happens with governments and large programmes.

Now it needs a sharper second avatar.

The PM could identify perhaps 20–25 cities, bring together India’s best architects, urban planners and administrators, and make them demonstrable models of excellent municipal governance.

You do not need to transform every Indian city simultaneously. First create examples that prove it can be done—particularly in BJP-governed states.

2. Government school education

Anyone closely connected with ground realities knows the condition of many state government schools.

This has persisted for decades, across parties and governments, and India should no longer accept it as inevitable. It starts seriously with Nehru Ji- he is often blamed for ignoring school education.

Improving state schools should become a major national political ambition, pursued with willing state governments, measurable outcomes and clear deadlines. 

Again, a few states producing dramatically better results can establish a benchmark for the rest of India.

3. Environment and urban green spaces

This is both a quality-of-life issue and one that fits naturally with India’s civilisational emphasis on harmony with nature.

Cities need serious programmes for tree cover, neighbourhood green spaces and large urban “oxygen zones”—not merely symbolic plantation drives, but sustained ecological improvement.

These may sound like softer issues than national security, infrastructure or macroeconomics.

But they shape everyday life—and therefore shape how young Indians experience the country.

A young person may not distinguish between what is constitutionally the responsibility of the Centre, a state government or a municipality. When one political party governs across several of these levels, dissatisfaction inevitably travels upward.

That is why these issues should be taken head-on.

There is also a larger communication point.

Viksit Bharat 2047 is an important national horizon, but 2047 is psychologically very far away—especially for someone who is 20 today.

A long-term vision needs shorter missions within it: concrete national goals for 2030, 2032, 2035 and beyond.

People stay engaged when they can see milestones being crossed.

The next phase could also be presented as a natural progression from the first decade.

From 2014 onward, the focus was necessarily on foundational questions: national security, border infrastructure, highways and expressways, financial inclusion, housing, sanitation, basic economic architecture, digital infrastructure, the space sector and state capacity.

Much of that work must continue.

But the next chapter can increasingly focus on the quality of everyday Indian life:

Better cities.
Better schools.
Cleaner and greener neighbourhoods.
Political renewal does not always require a new slogan or a new medium.
Sometimes it requires a new governing mission. Talk on issues youngsters relate to, unlike just copying their lingo and communication methodology. Once issues are addressed, they will become your warriors taking the msg forward in their style. Style can be tweaked, but not without producing original content.

The answer to a content problem cannot simply be more differently styled content

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.
Credit : TRP/RJ Raunac.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Amid heightened tensions and a heavy police presence in Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan state in India, the local administration has begun demolishing a 44-year-old historic mosque. The operation was carried out on Sunday (June 7) to remove the historic Noorani Mosque, located in the Malviya Nagar area of Jaipur.

The four-story Noorani Mosque located in Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, India, is being demolished by the authorities as part of a road-widening project. In connection with the operation, internet services across the city were suspended for 24 hours, and extensive security measures were put in place.

The Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) claims that the mosque was constructed illegally on leased land. However, the mosque committee has rejected this allegation, stating that the land was legally purchased from a housing society in 1981 before the structure was built.

A large number of police personnel have been deployed in and around the area, drone surveillance is being conducted, and restrictive orders remain in effect throughout the operation. The mosque committee and several opposition lawmakers have criticized the move, alleging that proper procedures were not followed.

Authorities stated that the temporary internet shutdown was imposed to prevent the spread of rumors and misinformation and to maintain law and order during the demolition process. So far, the operation has remained peaceful, with no reports of violence or unrest.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

The "Weekend of Blood" —
Situating the January 2026 Iran Massacre within the Global History of State Violence

The events of January 8–9, 2026, in the Islamic Republic of Iran represent a catastrophic inflection point in the global history of state violence. In this document, we argue that the verified floor of the death toll of Iranian protesters during the January 2026 crackdown in Iran is not only unprecedented in Iran, but also represents a statistically unique and extreme anomaly in the history of state violence against civilian protest movements worldwide.

Data: Establishing The Verified Floor
The high-end estimates of the 2026 Iran massacre, as reported by several reputable international media outlets surpass 30,000 deaths [1, 2]. However, to analyze the scale of this violence, we look at the most conservative, verified data rather than the fluctuating high-end estimates. As of February 1st, 2026, the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) has confirmed the identities of a total of 6,842 victims within the first thirty-six days of the protests, with the vast majority occurring during the January 8–9 window [3]. Among those, HRANA reports recording 6,425 individuals as “protesters”, including 146 minors; 214 as members of government‑affiliated forces and 57 as “civilian non‑protesters” [3]. An additional 11,280 deaths remain under review by HRANA at the time of writing this report [3]. In this report, we will use the 6,842 figure as it represents the "verified floor"—individuals whose identities and deaths have been meticulously documented despite the intentional disruption of the internet in Iran.

Simultaneously, the Iranian government’s officially admitted toll—typically used as a tool of downplaying atrocities—stands at 3,117 deaths. This figure is substantially lower than independent tallies, reflecting consistent under‑reporting in official statistics [4].

What Makes This A “Crime Against Humanity”?
The classification of the January 2026 crackdown as Crimes Against Humanity is supported by a burgeoning international legal consensus. According to the Rome Statute [5], such crimes consist of acts—including murder, imprisonment, and torture—committed as part of a 'widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population.' The Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI) and Amnesty International have documented that the 2026 massacre was not a series of scattered escalations, but a "coordinated nationwide escalation" in the use of lethal force [6, 7]. This is evidenced by the "organized" state response across "all 31 of Iran’s provinces," involving the simultaneous deployment of military-grade weaponry—including "DShK machine guns" and "snipers" positioned on rooftops [6, 8]. Furthermore, the state implemented what observers describe as a systematic targeting of medical neutrality, where security forces "removed wounded protesters from hospitals," "fired into the faces of victims at close range," and carried out the "arrests and prosecutions of doctors" treating the injured [6, 8]. The CHRI asserts that the "intensity and rate of the mass killings," characterized by the deliberate "targeting of protesters' heads and torsos," meets the threshold for international atrocity crimes [6, 7]. This legal standing was solidified by the UN Human Rights Council's emergency resolution on January 23, which extended the Fact-Finding Mission’s mandate specifically to investigate these crimes under international law [8].

Comparative Historical Analysis
The lethal intensity of the 2026 crackdown is unprecedented in the Islamic Republic’s history of violently suppressing dissent since 1979 [6]. The 2026 massacre follows the precedent of 'Bloody November' in 2019 in Iran, where a total telecommunication blackout facilitated a five-day crackdown that resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,500 protesters according to Interior Ministry officials—a figure that, while significantly lower than current investigative estimates, was the bloodiest suppression in the country since the 1979 Revolution [9].

The 2026 massacre is a calculated repetition of the "Bloody November" strategy of 2019. In both instances, the violence was inextricably linked to a total national internet and telecommunications blackout, to facilitate mass killing away from international scrutiny.  By severing the logic layer of the network and jamming satellite signals, the regime decoupled the act of killing from the global community's ability to witness it in real-time [10]. This repeated use of “Digital Blackout” to facilitate mass killing is an instrument of impunity by design [11]. Under international legal standards, such a coordinated effort should be interpreted as a hallmark of systematic intent to commit atrocity crimes.

To situate the January 8–9 events within global history of state violence against civilian protest movements, we use data collected by the Nonviolent and Violent Campaigns and Outcomes (NAVCO) project. Historical data suggests that between 1946 and 2013, the average unarmed revolution suffered approximately 105 deaths per year [12]. While regimes respond with lethal force in nearly 88% of nonviolent uprisings, "mass killings"—defined as episodes where at least 1,000 unarmed civilians are killed—occur in only about 23% of cases [12].

The international community has historically used the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre as the primary reference point for state-led suppression of domestic protest. In the historical massacre at Tiananmen Square (1989), the death toll was estimated to be "hundreds to thousands" [12]. An official report issued by the Chinese authorities claimed that “more than 3,000 civilians were wounded and over 200, including 36 college students, died during the riot”, according to Amnesty International [13]. Whereas the Red Cross Society of China reportedly provided an early estimate of Approx. 2,600 deaths, based on data collected from various hospitals in Beijing [14]. Therefore, the Iran crackdown exceeds the confirmed lethality of the 1989 crackdown in Beijing.

The toll also far exceeds other notorious crackdowns [12]. In Egypt, during the Rabaa Massacre (2013), following the coup against Mohammed Morsi, the Egyptian Army massacred nearly 1,000 Muslim Brotherhood activists who were protesting [12]. In the Amritsar Massacre (1919), British colonial forces in India fired into a crowd of nonviolent protesters, killing hundreds (cited as 200–300 in colonial records) and injuring over 1,000  [12]. During the Dili Massacre (1991), Indonesian forces killed approximately 250 civilians in East Timor attending a funeral for an independence activist [12]. In the Khartoum Massacre in Sudan (2019) Security forces stormed a protest camp, killing over 100 people and dumping bodies in the Nile River  [12].

While the Syrian Revolution (2011–2026) resulted in over 230,000 deaths, those casualties were the product of a fifteen-year multi-front civil war involving heavy artillery, air raids, and foreign intervention. Even when compared to the bloodiest "crackdown phases" of the Syrian uprising, such as the Daraya or Ghouta massacres, the scale of the Iranian event is distinct. The most lethal single-day atrocity of the Syrian Revolution—the 2013 Ghouta chemical attack, which claimed approximately 1,429 lives according to U.S. intelligence assessments [15]. Unlike the gradual escalation of the Syrian Revolution (2011) or the localized horrors of the Srebrenica massacre (1995), the January 2026 violence in Iran should be characterized by an unprecedented "lethality-to-time" ratio, given that it was a singular, state-led massacre executed against a domestic civilian population within a non-war setting.

Conclusion & Call to Action
At the time of writing this report, the verified floor of casualties (6,842) already reveals a concentration of state lethality in a single weekend that is statistically more intense than any comparable domestic suppression event in modern history. This represents a quantitative and qualitative shift in state violence that the world has yet to fully grasp.

Once the investigative estimates by HRANA are eventually confirmed, the lethality of the 2026 Iran Massacre may exceed the confirmed lethality of events like Tiananmen (1989) by an order of magnitude, standing as the deadliest state-led crackdown on a domestic protest movement in a singular event in at least the last 100 years of global history!
To prevent this "Silence-Kill" protocol from becoming a global blueprint for impunity, the international community must transition from condemnation to an active protection strategy, centered on three urgent pillars:

First, the international community must treat the ongoing internet disruption in Iran as a primary tactical weapon of the massacre. We call for Digital Humanitarian Intervention, including the mass deployment of satellite-based technologies to restore the "witness layer" and neutralize the regime’s military-grade jamming and restore the digital sovereignty of Iranians.

Second, the world must confront the Judicial Blockade surrounding the “expedited” prosecution of nearly 49,070 detainees [16], including many medical staff and lawyers [17]. Unverified claims made by the US president regarding the suspension of executions [18] must not distract from the reality that the Iranian judiciary has explicitly urged punishment "as quickly as possible" and "without leniency," utilizing the capital charge of Moharebeh (“enmity against God”) to facilitate state-sanctioned murder [8].

Finally, because the Iranian state has actively weaponized its sovereignty to commit mass murder, the criteria for the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) have been met. Under the R2P framework, when a state is the manifest perpetrator of crimes against humanity, the international community’s responsibility to intervene becomes mandatory, and protecting the rights of individuals takes precedence over the sovereignty of hostile states ruling over them. This warrants the immediate activation of international justice mechanisms, including the pursuit of universal jurisdiction and a formal referral to the International Criminal Court.

If the international community continues to view these events through the lens of "unrest" rather than a singular, concentrated massacre that is a clear departure from the historical norms of the 21st-century, it risks normalizing unprecedented levels of state violence.

4. यदि Cash Payment स्वीकार करना विभागीय नियमों के अनुसार अनुमत है, तो C.R. Park Post Office में ग्राहकों से Cash लेने से मना करने का कारण क्या है?

5. दिनांक 10.08.2026 को पूरे दिन Server Down रहने का वास्तविक कारण क्या था? क्या यह Department का Central Server/System Issue था या स्थानीय Post Office का Internet/Hardware/Software संबंधी मामला था?

6. Server Down होने की स्थिति में ग्राहकों को वैकल्पिक व्यवस्था उपलब्ध कराने के लिए विभाग द्वारा क्या Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) निर्धारित है?

7. कृपया यह भी जांच की जाए कि Server/Online System बार-बार प्रभावित होने की स्थिति में ग्राहकों को अनावश्यक रूप से परेशान तो नहीं किया जा रहा है।

मैं यह भी स्पष्ट करना चाहता हूँ कि Department of Posts एक महत्वपूर्ण सार्वजनिक सेवा है। Digital Payment को बढ़ावा देना अलग विषय है, लेकिन यदि किसी सेवा में Cash Payment स्वीकार करने पर कोई प्रतिबंध लगाया गया है तो उसका स्पष्ट एवं लिखित विभागीय आधार होना चाहिए। केवल मौखिक रूप से ग्राहकों को यह कहना कि “Cash नहीं चलेगा, केवल Online Payment होगा” उचित नहीं होना चाहिए, जब तक इसके संबंध में सक्षम प्राधिकारी का स्पष्ट आदेश/निर्देश उपलब्ध न हो।

अतः निवेदन है कि इस मामले की उच्च स्तर पर जांच कराई जाए तथा C.R. Park Post Office के संबंधित अधिकारियों से स्पष्टीकरण लिया जाए।

साथ ही, कृपया मुझे निम्नलिखित जानकारी उपलब्ध कराने की कृपा करें:

- 10.08.2026 को Server Down रहने का कारण।
- Server Down की अवधि एवं संबंधित Technical Complaint/Ticket Number।
- Cash Payment स्वीकार न करने के संबंध में लागू Circular/Order/Guideline की प्रति।
- क्या यह व्यवस्था पूरे Delhi Postal Circle में लागू है या केवल C.R. Park Post Office में?

कृपया शिकायत पर की गई कार्रवाई से मुझे लिखित रूप में अवगत कराया जाए।

“Scanner de dijiye.”
“UPI kar deta hoon.”

These have become some of the most ordinary sentences in Indian life. That ordinariness is the achievement. Successful infrastructure is not technology displayed as spectacle; it is technology absorbed into everyday life and trusted without a second thought.

Exactly ten years ago, UPI was rolled out. India did not merely introduce another way to pay, it began transforming the relationship between citizens, commerce and money.

As a Chartered Accountant, I tend to trust numbers more than adjectives. In FY 2016–17, UPI processed approximately 1.8 crore transactions worth about ₹0.07 lakh crore. By FY 2025–26, that had risen to 24,161 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore.

In July 2026 alone, UPI processed 2,365 crore transactions worth ₹29.88 lakh crore: an average of approximately 76.3 crore transactions every day.

These figures tell us how far UPI has travelled.

UPI’s real achievement is that it made sophisticated financial infrastructure almost invisible. The same interoperable payments rail now serves a street vendor and a large retailer. A small entrepreneur receives money instantly. A family can transfer funds across the country in seconds. A student in a hostel can receive ₹500 from home before the phone call ends.

By June 2026, UPI had onboarded 55.49 crore users. The Government has also reported that it serves 6.5 crore merchants, while 741 banks were live on the platform by July. During FY 2025–26, UPI accounted for nearly 86% of India’s retail payment transactions by volume. An IMF Fintech Note describes it as the world’s largest retail fast payment system by volume.

Under Prime Minister @narendramodi Ji’s Digital India vision, India did not merely catch up with the digital revolution. We showed the world how technology could be built at population scale, made interoperable and delivered to the last mile.

#10YearsOfUPI is therefore not merely a celebration of an app. It is a celebration of public digital infrastructure, institutional trust and inclusion by design. 🇮🇳

text:
Save Jharkhand’s Forests — Not Just Tie Rakhis Around Them

[The New Indian Express — Three lakh trees in Jharkhand to get ‘rakhis’ under forest conservation drive]
https://t.co/9lLeA10WqE

Jharkhand’s Forest Department has launched a month-long campaign under which rakhis will be tied to three lakh trees across 24 districts, presenting it as a community-driven forest-conservation initiative. The department says the campaign has helped villages protect trees and that Jharkhand’s forest cover has increased over the past two decades. 

But here is the uncomfortable question:

What good is tying a rakhi to a tree if the machinery of the state cannot protect forests from illegal mining?

This is not an imaginary problem. In May 2026, the Jharkhand High Court recorded serious concerns over illegal mining and found that enforcement by the Pollution Control Board, district administration, police and mining authorities had fallen short of the proactive vigilance required to curb a decade-long crisis. The Court ordered action against illegal operations, recovery of illegally extracted minerals, environmental compensation under the “Polluter Pays” principle, and reclamation of abandoned or illegally operated mines. 

The Court had already directed restrictions on stone mining and stone crushers near forest and forest-land boundaries, along with constant vigilance against unauthorised mining. 

Even the state government's own recent CAMPA review acknowledges the ecological threat: Chief Minister Hemant Soren noted that crushers in hilly areas and coal extraction in forest regions can disrupt wildlife habitats and movement, and called for a concrete balance between development and wildlife conservation. 

So the issue is not whether a symbolic Raksha Sutra is culturally meaningful. It can be—especially when communities themselves participate in protecting trees.

The problem arises when symbolism substitutes for enforcement.

Jharkhand does not merely need photographs of officials tying threads around trees.

It needs:

ruthless action against illegal mining and illegal crushers;

transparent publication of mining and environmental violations;

restoration of degraded forest and mining areas;

strict implementation of court-ordered environmental compensation;

protection of tribal and forest-dependent communities;

independent monitoring of forest diversion and mining permissions; and

public accountability for officials who repeatedly fail to enforce environmental law.

The government itself says Jharkhand has around 23,765.78 sq km of forest cover, nearly 29.81% of its geographical area.  That is precisely why protecting the state's ecological wealth cannot be reduced to ceremonial gestures.

Tie the rakhi if communities find meaning in it.
But then enforce the law.
Stop illegal mining.
Restore the damaged land.
Protect the forests.

Nature does not need a photo-op.

It needs protection.

Reference reporting

The New Indian Express — three-lakh-tree Raksha Bandhan conservation campaign. 

Jharkhand High Court — directions and observations concerning illegal mining, environmental damage and enforcement failures. 

Government of Jharkhand — CM's CAMPA review and acknowledgement of mining/crusher impacts on forests and wildlife. 

Jharkhand Forest Department / FSI data on forest cover. 

PIB — 2026 enforcement operations recovering illegally mined coal in Jharkhand and West Bengal.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India Orders Immediate Takedown of Dhruv Rathee’s (@dhruv_rathee)  Video.

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, Government of India, has passed an Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026) directing YouTube to remove the video titled “Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed” within 24 hours of receiving the Order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it has been uploaded today (19 July 2026).

Key points from the GAC Order:

- The video contains deliberate and malicious statements insulting Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.

- It falsely claims they consumed meat (including deer meat) and alcohol, using distorted references from scriptures.

- Such content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is against societal harmony.

- YouTube’s arguments on “free speech” were not accepted. Freedom of expression comes with reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order was issued after Hon'ble Delhi High Court’s direction on 3rd July 2026 to decide the appeal within 15 days.

Important: This observation and finding by the GAC that the video hurts religious sentiments will also have a strong bearing on the decision of the Ld. Magistrate before whom our petition seeking registration of FIR against Dhruv Rathee is pending for hearing on 10.09.2026.

Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of “content creation.” Justice is being delivered step by step.

In a significant legal update, tech giant Google has informed the Delhi High Court that a controversial video uploaded by popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been officially withheld from viewers across India. The dispute centers around a video titled “Can Hindus Eat BEEF? | Kerala Story 2 EXPOSED”, which Rathee uploaded in March.

Advocate @SachdevaAmita (Amita Sachdeva) filed a petition alleging that the video contained “false, misleading, and provocative statements” claiming that Hindu deities Lord Ram, Lord Krishna, and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol. She argued this severely hurt the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus.

Following a High Court order to expedite the grievance on July 3, the Central Government's Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) directed Google on July 15 to remove the video within 24 hours.

The petitioner has pushed for a global injunction, pointing out that the video remains accessible globally and via Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) inside India, viewing geo-blocking as “partial compliance”.

Presiding Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma noted that Google has executed what it can under current domestic boundaries, as the broader legal issue regarding global takedown mandates is already pending before a separate Division Bench of the High Court.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the government, argued that offensive videos should be blocked across the board to avoid a repetitive game of legal cat-and-mouse with duplicates. The court has adjourned the matter for its next hearing on September 3.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.
