Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

WHEN CHILDREN NEED TO WADE THROUGH FLOODWATER TO REACH SCHOOL, CALL IT WHAT IT IS: ADMINISTRATIVE FAILURE

The image of children making their way through floodwater to reach school is not a symbol of “development”. It is a warning about the most basic responsibility of a government: keeping citizens, especially children, safe.

Prayagraj has faced severe waterlogging after days of heavy rain. Roads and low-lying areas were submerged, drains overflowed, and student accommodation was affected. The crisis became serious enough for the Allahabad High Court to take suo motu cognisance, summon senior officials and question why preventive measures had not been taken in advance. 

The Court subsequently directed authorities to deploy sufficient pumps and clear affected low-lying areas within 24 hours. 

Schools themselves were forced to close because of the dangerous conditions, while waterlogging continued to affect educational institutions and students. At CMP Degree College, students and teachers protested after water remained for more than a week, with allegations that overflowing drains and sewage were feeding into the campus. 

Yes, extraordinary rainfall can overwhelm any city. But that cannot become a permanent excuse for predictable, recurring failures of drainage and urban planning.

A government is not judged only by flyovers, highways, statues or slogans.

It is judged by whether a child can walk to school without having to cross filthy floodwater.

Children deserve safe roads, functioning drainage and dignity — not speeches about development.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

Indian propaganda accounts are falsely claiming that Pakistan has slowed down production of the JF-17 Block III fighter jet. The claim is misleading and not backed by evidence.

Production Status
By mid-2025, Pakistan has already produced around 23 Block III jets, with the Kamra facility on track to complete the full 30-unit order. This shows production is proceeding as planned, not “slowed down” as alleged.

Export Success
Far from lacking orders, Pakistan has secured a landmark deal with Azerbaijan for 40 JF-17 Block III jets. This is one of Pakistan’s biggest defense export agreements, proving both the demand and credibility of the aircraft on the global stage.

Cost Reality
The figure of $55 million per jet is misleading. That price includes weapons, training, spare parts, and support packages. The base cost of the jet itself remains around $25 million, making it one of the most cost-effective 4.5 generation fighters available.

The narrative pushed by Indian disinformation accounts is baseless. The JF-17 Block III program remains on schedule, expanding Pakistan’s air power and earning major international contracts. Rather than being “slowed,” the aircraft has become a symbol of Pakistan’s growing aerospace industry and defense exports.

If you're stuck around 20% margin...

The solution is usually owning the products already selling rather than hunting for a new one.

Dropshipping and holding stock solve completely different problems, and running both at once is where the margin is.

The split looks like this:

- 70% stays pure dropship. That's your testing lane. New products, new angles, zero capital tied up, unlimited shots on goal.
- 30% is your own stock. Only proven bestsellers get in. Higher margin, custom packaging, faster shipping, fewer refunds.

The gap between those 2 models is bigger than people realise.

Dropship margins generally sit in the 15 to 30% range.

Private label brands tend to land at 50 to 70%, because you're buying direct and pricing on your own positioning instead of competing against 30 other stores listing the identical item.

What that does at €1,500 a day in revenue:

At 22% margin that's about €330 profit a day, so roughly €9,900 a month.

At 34% it's about €510 a day, or €15,300 a month.

That's €180 a day, which looks like nothing daily and turns into €5,400 a month.

Identical revenue, ad spend, and store.

You didn't find a new winner.

You just started getting paid properly for the one you already had.

How you actually run it:

1/ Pick your bestseller.

Consistent sales over a meaningful period, not one strong week. Never stock something you're hoping will work.

2/ Ask your supplier for a stock price.

Buying volume gets you a lower unit cost than the dropship rate, and that break is a big chunk of the margin gain.

3/ Add your packaging.

Your logo on the box or the mailer.

Cheap, and it turns a generic product into your brand.

4/ Start small.

Around 50 units is a normal starting point depending on your supplier's MOQ.

Prove the flow first, then reorder.

5/ Store it in China.

You don't need a European warehouse.

Keeping stock at your supplier or a Chinese fulfilment centre is cheaper, and shipping still improves because units are pre-picked.

6/ Reorder when it runs out.

Sold out means proven, so buy the next batch. That's the whole loop.

Before you commit money to any batch, run through this:

- Has it sold consistently, or did it just have one good week
- Do you know your real break-even ROAS on it, refunds included
- Is the refund and quality rate low enough to justify capital
- Can you afford the batch without touching your ad budget
- Did you order and physically check a sample
- Do you have a reorder trigger set before you sell out

The mistake that kills this is stocking something because you like it, or because of one strong week.

Inventory turns a bad product decision into dead capital sitting in a warehouse.

That's exactly what the 70% lane is for.

You never have to guess which products earn a place in the 30%, because the testing already told you.

None of this is advanced.

It's buying your proven winners in small batches and putting your name on them, for the margin those winners should have been paying you the whole time.

Lagrange's trigonometric identities ✍️

This are one of those lovely mathematical discoveries which, on the surface, appears utterly complicated but in fact reveals a neat and elegant truth lying beneath all that seems messy and disorderly. In order to see what these identities are asserting, you first have to consider the unit circle, that is, a circle with a radius of exactly one unit placed at the centre of a flat coordinate plane. This circle is the setting in which the whole thing takes place and it is linked to trigonometry in a deep and beautiful manner. Any point located on the circumference of this circle can be fully described by an angle; if that angle is denoted by A, then the horizontal position of the point is given by the cosine of A and the vertical position by the sine of A. 

This means that cosine and sine are not merely abstract mathematical functions but actually represent the horizontal and vertical coordinates of points on the circle, which is the fundamental geometric basis of trigonometry. Now suppose that you place two points anywhere on the edge of this unit circle, one at angle A and the other at angle B, and then put to yourself two simple geometric questions. The first of these is: if you draw arrows from the centre of the circle to each of the two points and then add those arrows together by the usual rule of vector addition  that is, by joining the tail of one to the tip of the other to obtain a single resultant arrow what is the length of that resultant arrow? The second question is: if you draw a straight line from one point directly to the other across the circle, what is the length of that line, which mathematicians refer to as a chord? These two questions seem as though they should have complicated answers depending on all the particular details of where each point is situated on the circle, but the remarkable thing that Lagrange's identities show is that the answers depend on just one factor, namely the difference between the two angles, and are given by remarkably simple formulas involving trigonometric functions of half that angular difference. The first identity, known as the sum identity, answers the first question about the combined arrow and states that the square of the length of the resultant vector is equal to four times the square of the cosine of half the difference between the two angles. You can at once check that this works in the extreme cases. 

When both points are at the same place on the circle, so that the two angles are equal, the two arrows point in the same direction and add up perfectly to give a resultant of length two, so the square of the length should be four. Half the angular difference is zero, the cosine of zero is one, and four times one squared is four, which is exactly correct. When the two points are exactly opposite each other on the circle, so that the arrows point in precisely opposite directions, they completely cancel one another out and the resultant has zero length, so the square of the length should be zero. Half the angular difference is a quarter of a rotation, the cosine of a quarter rotation is zero, and four times zero squared is zero, which is also correct. For all the cases in between these two extremes, the formula gives the right answer precisely. The second identity, referred to as the difference identity, answers the second question about the chord and says that the square of the length of the chord joining the two points is equal to four times the square of the sine of half the angular difference. Once again you can easily verify the extreme cases. When the points coincide, the chord has zero length, half the angular difference is zero, the sine of zero is zero, and four times zero squared is zero, which is correct.

It’s safe to say that the world changed a lot in the last five years. It certainly did for me. After putting out Total Freedom in 2020 then accepting the fact that touring it and promoting it wasn’t going to happen, I went back to my coffee shop and worked, I got married, I moved (twice), and I even found myself living in a new country.

When the summer of 2022 rolled in, I was able to make up for lost time on the road until 2023 when I was ready to head to St. Petersburg, Florida and take some well-earned time to write. It was in early 2024 after sending him my cover version of his song “Traveling Alone” that Jason Isbell and I first talked about working together, and incredibly he offered to produce these songs, enlisting Gena Johnson as co-producer. 

Pinch me.

Fast forward to September 2024 - Jason, Gena and I started making this album at Sound Emporium in Nashville. Jason enlisted members of the 400 Unit to be our rhythm section. We recorded the songs that eventually became the 10 tracks on “Billionaire”. I am so indebted and thankful to Jason and Gena for their dedication, their time, their care and their talents - in championing me and my work, and to all the musicians who appear on this album coming out August 22nd. 

It’s true when they say your songs are like your children and you can’t pick favorites (not out loud, at least).  But I love the two we’re putting out today.  “Save Your Soul” and “Say Goodbye, Tell No One” kick off this album sonically the way I had hoped my new record would sound - tough and cool, vulnerable and honest.

My favorite songwriters and bands are written all over my work, for which I am unapologetic.  Songs that tell the story of looking through the rear view mirror on my way to something new, watching a version of myself and my life behind me get smaller on the horizon as I go. I found the last five years fraught with challenges of all kinds, highs and lows, profound grief, grit and determination, anger and even unabashed joy in my new locale (and very tanned legs). 

Thanks for listening and staying tuned for all the ones that will be released in the coming weeks.  For the foreseeable future, I will be touring with my band, an exceptional group of musicians who are my best friends and we plan on burning down the fucking house every night thank you very much.  

Here we go.

So swing by and stream the songs, check out the show calendar, pre-order some vinyl and check out some of the goodies we’ve put together for you.

THANK YOU.

I found some old journal entries. This one is probably circa ~2006, just titled "Scrap:"

I moved to Pittsburgh at the right time in my life, but at the wrong time of year.  Coming from the west coast, I was actually naive enough to be excited about the prospect of winter.  I imagined nothing but snowball fights, snow angles, icicles on the eves, and that muffled crunch of loose snow under your feet. I thought I'd be doing nothing but riding sleds and watching snowflakes drift down past the street lights at night.  It turns out, however, that winter doesn't quite resemble this fantasy, and that it's also the kind of thing you really want to ease into.  The house we moved into didn't have working utilities, much less effective heating, and January wasn't the best time to be standing in the basement with a pipe wrench, doing my best to install gas lines without being able to feel my fingers.  There were days when I literally couldn't apply the thread sealant to the black iron, because it had frozen in the tube.

So we had this house, and it was a wreck, and it was well below zero.  But it was beautiful that we had anything at all.  Just like a squat, the first order of business was to get something that approximated a flushing toilet.  After that, we started tearing out walls, putting in plumbing, and trying to eek everything that we could out of forgotten pallets and scrap lumber.

At one point we pulled a cast-iron bathtub out of a bathroom, and not having any immediate place to put it, temporarily set it outside -- right up against the back of the house.  The next morning I stepped out back, and it was gone.  Totally vanished.  It hadn't even been 24 hours, and somehow a really heavy cast-iron bathtub had disappeared from our back yard.  It seemed like such a random theft -- who in their right mind would spontaneously coordinate an operation to move something of that size?

I didn't yet realize that where San Francisco has scroungers, Pittsburgh has scrappers.  The hunt isn't for kitchy coffee mugs or spare furniture.  It's for raw metals.

So several months later when we pulled out another cast-iron bathtub, this one with a large hole rusted through the bottom of it, I knew just how to get rid of it.  We simply put it in the back yard.

The next day I was looking out the window when I saw an old pickup truck drive through the ally.  It had all kinds of metal pipes and appliance parts jutting out the plywood sides which had been erected to try and contain as much metal in the bed of the truck as possible.  Two guys hopped out, sized up the tub, and wrangled it into the truck.  They continued around the block and pulled up next to a dumpster that we'd been steadily filling with moldy carpet out front. I waved.

"ALRIGHT IF WE PULL THIS DUCTWORK OUT OF THIS DUMPSTER?!"

"No problem at all."

Upon closer inspection, these two were quite the team.  One bulky, one scrappy, both getting old.  They almost reminded you of something out of a Walter Matthou movie, where they'd both gone hard of hearing, so all communication between them was done by yelling -- even if they were standing only inches apart.  I gathered that one was named Ron, the other Wade, and that their voices were continually horse.

After they'd gotten the ductwork into the truck, one of them looked the house up and down.  "SAY, YOU GOT ANYTHING ELSE IN THERE?"  

"Well," I said, "we do have an old broken gas furance in the basement."

Wade looked at Ron.  "YOU WANNA GO CHECK IT OUT RON?" 

"ALRIGHT I'LL GO CHECK IT OUT!"

So Ron followed me down into the basement.  He jerked the furnace around to get a feel for the weight, nodded to himself, and counted the steps up to the first floor.  Back outside, Ron and Wade had a quick conference.

"HOW'S IT LOOK RON?"
"IT'S HEAVY WADE. REAL HEAVY. 17 STEPS."

They mulled it over, before turning to where I was standing two feet away and yelling "ALRIGHT WE'LL DO IT." 

I went down with them, to supervise, but was quickly roped into the heavy lifting.  The first thing I noticed was that moving scrap for a living doesn't make you a very good mover.  They didn't even bother trying to tip the furnace down, and instead just knocked the thing straight over with a resounding crash.  We sort of carry/dragged it over to the steps, where the real work began.

The stairway from the basement back up to the first floor is just wide enough for the furnace.  There are 13 steps up, then a small landing for a 180degree turn, then the remaining 4 steps to the first floor.  Our original linup was with Wade (the big one) in front of the furnace, with me and Ron (the scrappy ones) below the furnace.

These guys were not afraid to make noise.  Every time they went to lift, they were moaning or yelling or cursing almost embarrasingly loudly.  We tried moving it up a few steps before Wade finally shouted "RON! YOU KNOW I CAN'T DO THIS! I'VE ONLY GOT THREE TOES!"

I wondered if I'd heard Wade correctly, and he responded "the sugars" when I looked at him somewhat quizzically. 

So Ron and Wade traded places, such that now Ron was in front and I was down below with the big guy.  In fact, both him and I could barely fit in the stairwell at the same time.  We'd lift a step at a time, and it took us a solid 45 minutes to make it up the first flight and into the landing.

The furnace just barely fit through the doorway from the stairwell to the landing, but a pipe jutting out of it got stuck in a wall.  So Wade and I were left standing on the basement side of the furnace, with the whole thing blocking the door, while Ron was out on the landing side of the furnace.

Suddenly, Wade turned to me and asked "HEY, IS THERE ANOTHER WAY OUT OF THIS BASEMENT?"

"Actually, no this is the only entrance."

He started looking around frantically.  "I... I... I GOTTA GET OUT OF HERE!  I'M CLAUSTRAUPHOBIC! GET ME THE FUCK OUT OF HERE!"

He continued yelling, but also started trying to pull the furnace back down towards us, which would have crushed us for sure.  I could barely fit in the starewall with Wade as it was, but now I was getting seriously squished up against the wall in all the hysterics.

I tried to calm him down, told him to take a deep breath, but nothing was working.  I couldn't decide whether I should continue trying to help work things out in the stairwell, or just bolt back down into the basement and take cover.  Ron peered through, saw what was happening, and yelled "I'LL GO GET THE AXE!"

"The what?" I thought.

"RON! YOU CAN'T LEAVE ME LIKE THIS! YOU CAN'T LEAVE ME!"

While the furnace did fit squarely in the door frame, there was a small 2ft gap between the top of the furnace and the top of the door frame.  "Wade!"  I yelled, "Wade! Why don't you try going over it!"

Without a microsecond of hesitation, this 250+lb guy immediately started scrambling up the furnace, trying to squeeze through the opening in the top.  I sort of shrugged to myself, sighed, then started pushing on his ass, trying to help wedge him through the opening.  Eventually the bulk of him was directly on top of the furnace, and when Ron came back he was able to help pull him through.  He then went down face-first over the other side.

But now I was stuck in the basement, with these two lunatics on the other side.  The offending pipe that was preventing the furnace from moving any further needed to be resolved, and Ron was holding a full-sized axe.  "Now Ron, I've got some wrenches in that room over there, you could-" WHAM! The axe came down on the pipe, ripping out a section of drywall along with it.

They jerked it around the bend, shoved it up the remaining steps, and it was out the front door.

"Say," I asked, "how much do you get for steel, anyway?"

"FOUR CENTS A POUND."

As an Indian did you celebrate Meta making Kunal Shah the boss of WhatsApp? And then immediately you thought how a foreign company is about to run the rails of 1.5 billion people?

China saw this coming and built WeChat (social feed, messaging, and payments fused into one platform, wired into how the state governs). But China's model is the CCP's model. One party, top-down control, surveillance as the default, dissent erased. That works for an authoritarian state. It's the opposite of what India is.

India is a liberal democracy. Many parties, free press that can taunt Modi’s 56 inches, and 1.5 billion people who are allowed to disagree out loud. So India can't just copy WeChat. As an Indian founder, can you build a platform that gives the state the tools to keep the peace in the world's most diverse country, without handing it a CCP-style kill switch? I think you can. I prototyped what it could look like.

You start with one truth: governing a country as diverse as India is, fundamentally, an exercise in managing information. One wrong post in the wrong town at the wrong hour becomes a riot. X and WhatsApp are built to resist the government intervention as they are US based companies. US is unique in the world when it comes to freedom of expression. So by default, X/WhatsApp don't bend for the local context. A platform tuned to India would do the opposite, without becoming a censorship machine. Here's how:

1. Graduated, time-bound information control with in-built accountability
The local administrator (the DM) can block a single post for up to 24 hours. Just long enough to defuse an emerging riot-like situation on the ground, immediately, while tempers cool. If they need longer, the system forces them to seek a one-week extension from the State's Chief Minister. And a permanent takedown can't be done locally at all. That request is channeled up to the Home Minister or CIC. This ensures that no one person can quietly bury something forever. Every level of control has a higher level watching it. This is the line between India and China. Not CCP “censorship but but control that is checked at every step.
2. Political hierarchy that mirrors India's actual structure.
Unlike China's one party, India has many. Some of these are regional and faith based. Irrespective of ideology, parties can build their real hierarchy inside the platform: national → state → district → block → village. The booth-level worker in a village and the national leadership are part of one verifiable chain, instead of a chaos of anonymous handles claiming to speak for a party. The structure is in built to transfer mantle of local MP to another person belong to a different party as new election results get declared. With Uttar Pradesh being the most politically active state, I think the app should start from UP. BJP, SP, and Congress provide enough fuel for rapid adoption.
3. Trust-based verification without intrusive government ID that fights bots.
Many LefT leaning Indians shame India for being a low-trust society. The reality is quite different. India is very high trust. The platform leverages this high trust for verification. Verification starts with officials and party representatives as the root authorities. But from there, anyone who is verified can verify people they personally know. No demand for a driving licence or Aadhaar to exist on the platform. No central database of who you are. The genius is in the accountability. Every verification leaves a trail. The moment a fake account is caught, the system analyzes who verified them and re-examines everyone that account went on to verify. Fraud, once detected, unravels the whole branch. That makes fake networks expensive to build and easy to squash.
4. Festivals, localized to your district where anyone can become a local celebrity.
India is a land of festivals, and festivals are deeply local. What one district celebrates isn't what the next one does. So every user picks their district, and the app's world is shaped around it. Folks in Saharanpur see their background change to Shakumbhari Devi in season, while folks in Meerut see Nauchandi. If you are a Muslim, your wallpaper says Eid Mubarak during Eid. Users still have a say in what they see, but the default is home. This turns festivals into community engines. On Diwali, people across a district post their rangoli, and neighbors from the same district upvote the ones they love. An ordinary person can become a local celebrity overnight, recognized by the people who actually live around them. A local batting star from Balia can catch eyes of state cricket team selectors after smashing 6-sixes in an over. And a state can lift this up a level, running the same celebration as a state-wide competition that builds community across districts. Festivals stop being a feed of strangers and become your town, at its best.
 5. Private messaging with the network you already trust. The same web of verified relationships that powers your feed also powers your inbox. Message your Nani two districts away or the school friend living next door, all within a network where the person on the other end is who they say they are. Because messaging rides on the same trust graph as verification, it inherits the same protection. The bot farms and unknown numbers that flood WhatsApp don't get a way in. Your conversations stay among the people who are actually part of your world, from family scattered across the state to the neighbor you've known since elementary school.

This is a WeChat designed for India's rich diversity and unique challenges. Fast where it needs to be, accountable where it must be, built on trust instead of surveillance, and rooted in the place you actually call home. Neither China's kill switch nor Silicon Valley's 3rd world arrogance. India's own.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

The cashless agenda is not a prediction. It is a scheduled implementation. The 2030 timeline is not a guess; it is the target date embedded in Agenda 2030, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) CBDC blueprints, and the World Economic Forum’s “Great Reset” paperwork.

You have already watched it happen. The end of cash is not being debated. It is being installed.

Cash Is Freedom. That Is Why It Must Die.

Physical cash is the last anonymous, off-grid, sovereign financial instrument.

· Cash cannot be frozen.
· Cash cannot be tracked.
· Cash cannot be taxed in real time.
· Cash cannot be remotely deactivated.
· Cash does not require a digital ID, a bank account, a phone, or permission.

That is exactly why the globalist machine hates it.

Once cash is gone, every transaction becomes visible, taxable, programmable, and revocable. The state and the bank become the gatekeeper of your survival.

What Full Cashlessness Actually Means

They will not announce the death of cash. They will simply make it unavailable, inconvenient, and eventually illegal.

Under the 2030 timeline, the finished system looks like this:

· Your salary, pension, benefits, and refunds go only into a bank-controlled digital wallet.
· That wallet is linked to your biometric digital ID.
· Physical cash is restricted, then taxed, then treated as suspicious.
· Cash withdrawals above small limits are blocked or reported.
· Bank branches and ATMs are removed from most areas.
· Merchants are legally permitted or forced to refuse cash.
· Central Bank Digital Currency becomes the default.
· Every purchase carries a digital trail.
· Your account can be frozen instantly, without a court order.

You will not be able to buy food, fuel, or medicine without the system’s permission.

The Real Technologies Behind It

This is not just “more digital payments.” It is a global financial prison architecture.

The names are not secret:

· Bank for International Settlements (BIS): The central bank of central banks, actively promoting global CBDC interoperability.
· International Monetary Fund (IMF): Pushing cashless policies as “financial inclusion.”
· World Economic Forum (WEF): Promoting the “you will own nothing” model, where all assets and money are licensed, not owned.
· Reserve Bank of India (RBI): Running the Digital Rupee pilots.
· European Central Bank (ECB): Preparing the Digital Euro.
· U.S. Federal Reserve: Deployed FedNow in 2023.
· Mastercard, Visa, Google Pay, Apple Pay, PayPal: The corporate toll collectors who profit from every transaction.

The CBDC is not just digital money. It is programmable money.

Your money can be programmed to expire. It can be programmed to work only for certain goods. It can be programmed to work only in certain locations. It can be denied based on your health status, your social credit score, or your political compliance.

The Timeline You Are Watching

· 2016: India’s demonetisation shock. The West accelerates “war on cash.”
· 2019–2020: COVID is used to demonize cash as dirty. Contactless payments are pushed as safety.
· 2021–2022: CBDC pilots begin. China expands Digital Yuan. Nigeria launches eNaira. India launches Digital Rupee pilot.
· 2023: U.S. launches FedNow. More countries introduce cash deposit and withdrawal restrictions.
· 2024–2026: Cash infrastructure collapses. Bank branches close. Instant payment systems dominate.
· 2030: Target completion. Cash becomes the exception, then the crime.

This is not a natural shift. It is a controlled demolition.

The Endgame

Once cash is gone, the last off-grid escape is removed.

· You cannot build a parallel economy.
· You cannot save anonymously.
· You cannot give money to someone without both parties being logged.
· You cannot flee the system with physical value in your pocket.
· You cannot survive a digital blackout or a frozen account.

The system will know what you buy, where you buy it, when you buy it, and who you gave money to. And because the money is programmable, the system can decide whether you are allowed to buy at all.

The non-compliant will not be arrested. They will simply be switched off.

Cashless society is not about convenience. It is not about fighting corruption or terrorism. Those are cover stories.

It is about total control of the human being through total control of the medium of survival.

2030 is the finish line. The infrastructure is already built. You are living through the transition right now.

The question is not whether cash will be removed.

The question is whether you will still have any financial sovereignty left when the last note is declared obsolete.

Wake up. The cage is being welded shut, one digital transaction at a time.

text:
A Delhi High Court order has once again had to remind the Grievance Appellate Committee to follow the timeline already prescribed under the IT Rules, 2021. On 20 August 2026, the Court directed the GAC to decide the appeal of content creator Riya, whose Instagram account #riaspeaks has over five lakh followers, within 30 days. Her appeal had already been pending for more than 42 days. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/26gA6SeMe0

The GAC is particularly important because it is supposed to provide users with an appellate remedy against intermediary decisions, including arbitrary or permanent account bans. Yet when an appeal itself remains pending beyond the prescribed period, a creator can be left with no meaningful remedy except approaching a High Court. The burden then falls on users and the judiciary alike. (6/7)

IFF had earlier suggested increasing the number of GACs to deal with the growing volume of appeals and making GAC orders publicly accessible, given the quasi-adjudicatory nature of their work. Neither has happened. We are assisting Riya through the appeal process and will continue to monitor the matter. (7/7)
Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX
